content: The use of topical fluoride in children has become increasingly common over time. However, excessive fluoride exposure during early childhood can lead to dental fluorosis in permanent teeth. Dental fluorosis is a condition characterized by changes in the appearance of tooth enamel, ranging from mild discoloration to more severe structural damage. The objective of this review was to investigate the relationship between the use of topical fluoride in young children and the risk of developing dental fluorosis in their permanent teeth. The review included a comprehensive search of multiple databases and trials registers, with the most recent search conducted on July 28, 2022. Studies included in the review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, cohort studies, case-control studies, and cross-sectional surveys. These studies compared various forms of topical fluoride, such as toothpaste, mouth rinses, gels, foams, paint-on solutions, and varnishes, to alternative fluoride therapies, placebos, or no intervention. The target population was children under six years of age. The primary outcome of interest was the prevalence of dental fluorosis in permanent teeth. Data were extracted and analyzed using standard Cochrane methodologies, and the certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 43 studies were included in the review, comprising three RCTs, four cohort studies, 10 case-control studies, and 26 cross-sectional surveys. The risk of bias was assessed, with most observational studies judged to have a high risk of bias, while some RCTs and other studies were found to have moderate concerns regarding bias. Key Findings: 1. Age at which children started toothbrushing with fluoride toothpaste: Evidence from two cohort studies (260 children) was highly uncertain regarding whether starting to use fluoride toothpaste at or before 12 months of age, compared to after 12 months, influenced the risk of fluorosis (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.98, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.81 to 1.18; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, evidence from one cohort study (3939 children) and two cross-sectional studies (1484 children) was very uncertain about the association between starting fluoride toothpaste use before or after 24 months (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.13; very low-certainty evidence) or before or after four years (Odds Ratio [OR] 1.60, 95% CI 0.77 to 3.35; very low-certainty evidence). 2. Frequency of toothbrushing with fluoride toothpaste: Two case-control studies (258 children) provided very uncertain evidence regarding whether brushing less than twice per day, compared to twice or more per day, was associated with fluorosis (OR 1.63, 95% CI 0.81 to 3.28; very low-certainty evidence). Two cross-sectional surveys (1693 children) suggested that brushing less than once per day, compared to once or more per day, might be associated with a reduced risk of fluorosis (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.74; low-certainty evidence). 3. Amount of fluoride toothpaste used for toothbrushing: Two case-control studies (258 children) provided very uncertain evidence regarding whether using less than half a brush of toothpaste, compared to half or more of the brush, influenced the risk of fluorosis (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.46; very low-certainty evidence). Evidence from cross-sectional surveys was similarly uncertain (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.28; 3 studies, 2037 children; very low-certainty evidence). 4. Fluoride concentration in toothpaste: Evidence from two RCTs (1968 children) indicated that using toothpaste with lower fluoride concentrations likely reduces the risk of fluorosis. For example, toothpaste with 550 parts per million (ppm) fluoride compared to 1000 ppm showed a reduced risk (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.99; moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, toothpaste with 440 ppm fluoride compared to 1450 ppm also showed a reduced risk (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.89; moderate-certainty evidence). Two case-control studies (258 children) provided very uncertain evidence regarding the association between fluoride concentrations below 1000 ppm, compared to concentrations of 1000 ppm or higher, and the risk of fluorosis (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.52; very low-certainty evidence). 5. Age at which topical fluoride varnish was applied: Evidence from one RCT (123 children) suggested that applying fluoride varnish before the age of four years, compared to no application, may result in little to no difference in the risk of fluorosis (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.31; low-certainty evidence). However, low-certainty evidence from two cross-sectional surveys (982 children) indicated that applying fluoride varnish before the age of four years might be associated with an increased risk of fluorosis (OR 2.18, 95% CI 1.46 to 3.25). Conclusions: The majority of the evidence identified mild dental fluorosis as a potential adverse effect of early exposure to topical fluoride. However, the certainty of evidence regarding the risk of fluorosis associated with the timing of fluoride varnish application, the frequency of toothbrushing, the amount of toothpaste used, and the age at which fluoride toothpaste use begins was low to very low. Moderate-certainty evidence from RCTs indicated that children who used toothpaste with 1000 ppm or higher fluoride concentrations from one to two years of age until five to six years of age likely had an increased risk of developing dental fluorosis in their permanent teeth. Given the ethical concerns, it is not feasible to conduct new RCTs specifically to assess the development of dental fluorosis. However, future RCTs focusing on caries prevention could include data on early-life fluoride exposure and evaluate fluorosis as a long-term outcome. In the absence of such studies, further research will rely on observational designs, with careful attention to minimizing bias through prospective controlled methodologies.
